title: GCD, LCM & Euclid
tagline: The Euclidean algorithm computes gcd in O(log min) — plus extended gcd for modular inverses.

intuition.analogy: Tiling a rectangle with the largest possible square tiles: repeatedly cut the largest square you can off the rectangle, and the leftover strip is a smaller rectangle. The side of the final perfect square is the gcd.
paragraphs: The greatest common divisor (gcd) of a and b is the largest number dividing both. Euclid's insight: gcd(a, b) = gcd(b, a mod b), because any common divisor of a and b also divides a mod b. Repeating shrinks the numbers fast until one becomes 0.
From gcd you get lcm = a / gcd(a, b) · b (divide first to avoid overflow). These underpin fraction reduction, periodicity, and modular math.
The extended Euclidean algorithm additionally finds integers x, y with a·x + b·y = gcd(a, b). When gcd is 1, x is the modular inverse of a mod b — essential for division under a prime modulus.
intuition.keyIdea: gcd(a, b) = gcd(b, a mod b); the remainders shrink geometrically, giving logarithmic time.

steps.title: Euclid's recursion
steps.detail: gcd(a, b) = b == 0 ? a : gcd(b, a mod b). Each step replaces (a, b) with (b, a mod b).

steps.title: LCM from GCD
steps.detail: lcm(a, b) = a / gcd(a, b) · b. Divide before multiplying to avoid overflow.

steps.title: Extended gcd
steps.detail: Track coefficients so a·x + b·y = gcd. The inverse of a modulo m (when gcd=1) is x mod m.

complexity.timeReason: Remainders shrink at least by a factor related to the golden ratio each two steps.
complexity.spaceReason: Constant variables; recursion adds a logarithmic stack.

pitfalls: lcm can overflow — divide by gcd before multiplying.
gcd(0, 0) is conventionally 0; handle zeros consistently.
Extended-gcd inverses can be negative — normalise with ((x % m) + m) % m.

dryRun.clickMoment: Each line replaces the larger number with a remainder that's strictly smaller — the values plummet (48→18→12→6) in just a few steps, which is why gcd is logarithmic, not linear.
